entities.summary:
Leonardo di Piero Dati (died March 25, 1425) was a prominent Italian friar and humanist, serving as the tenth Master of the Order of Preachers (Dominicans) from 1414 until his death. Born in Florence, Dati navigated the tumultuous period of the Western Schism, playing a crucial role in the Dominican Order's internal politics and contributing significantly to the intellectual currents of early Renaissance humanism. His leadership was marked by efforts to restore unity and discipline within the fractured order, aligning the Dominicans with the broader conciliar movement aimed at resolving the papal crisis.

Elected Master General at the Council of Constance in 1414, Dati immediately faced the formidable challenge of uniting a Dominican Order divided in its allegiance among competing popes. He actively participated in the Council, advocating for ecclesiastical reform and the resolution of the Schism. His tenure saw him travel extensively across Europe, visiting Dominican convents to enforce reforms, consolidate authority, and ensure doctrinal coherence. Beyond his administrative duties, Dati was a respected scholar, known for his classical erudition and theological writings, embodying the synthesis of monastic commitment and humanist intellectualism characteristic of the era.

Dati's legacy primarily rests on his efforts to preserve the integrity and mission of the Dominican Order during a period of profound ecclesiastical instability. His leadership helped steer the Dominicans through the complexities of the Western Schism, ensuring the order's continued influence in both spiritual and intellectual spheres. He fostered an environment where humanistic studies could flourish within the Dominican tradition, bridging medieval scholasticism with the emerging Renaissance intellectual landscape. His work contributed to the eventual re-establishment of a unified papacy and a more cohesive Dominican structure.
